video_title: WHAT NOBODY'S SEEING IN THE AI REBOUND...
gist: In a charts-only episode, Patrick Ceresna and Kevin Muir argue the post-election selloff is an AI/semiconductor bear market (NASDAQ -16%, semis -30%) with healthy breadth and rotation into defensives, warning that rallies may be a trap with a dot-com-style lagged broad-market top. A hot CPI drove a sharp hawkish repricing (SOFR, possible 50bp Fed hike) and a broad dollar breakout, gold remains in a bear market with 3,600/3,200 targets, and oil's 50% pullback is seen as a buyable dip with asymmetric upside.

themes.theme: AI/semis crash as sector rotation, not broad selloff

insights.claim: The post-election equity drawdown was concentrated in AI: the S&P 500 fell about 7% peak-to-trough, the NASDAQ about 16%, and the semiconductor index about 30%.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Damage is narrow; treat AI/semis as the bear market, not the whole index.
insights.quote: the semiconductor index from peak to trough dropped 30% during this period

insights.claim: Despite the AI selloff, market breadth (share of stocks above their 50-day moving average) improved to roughly 72%, the highest since January-February, indicating money rotated out of AI rather than into cash.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Rotation, not liquidation: defensive sectors are absorbing flows out of AI.
insights.quote: they haven't been going to cash. they have been reallocating and rebalancing portfolios

insights.claim: Health care, biotech and consumer staples have been making new highs while AI sold off, so holders of names like Walmart, Coca-Cola, Costco and Eli Lilly saw a great month rather than a correction.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Defensive leadership is the current tape; watch whether it cracks.

insights.claim: The key tell for the next few weeks is whether the safe-haven areas (staples, health care, Apple at 52-week highs) start rolling over; contagion from AI into those groups via liquidity would signal a broader selloff, and absent that a further leg down is not imminent.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Monitor defensive sectors as the trigger for a broad market decline.
insights.quote: observing in the next couple weeks whether this starts to roll over will be a huge tell

insights.claim: Nvidia lost about $2 trillion of market capitalization in 30 days in a washout tied to a scandal, leaving semiconductors grossly oversold and due for a technical retracement if the broader market stays stable.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Short-term oversold bounce in AI/semis is plausible; not a new bull trend.
insights.quote: this is thing wiped out $2 trillion dollars of market capitalization in 30 days

insights.claim: The six-month clean bull trend off the April lows has been technically violated: uptrend broken, CTA sell triggers likely hit, and realized volatility spiking.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Systematic de-risking flows have been triggered; regime has shifted from clean uptrend.

insights.claim: The first-day market reaction to the US election was actually up, as many professionals saw it as a market-clearing event, so claims that the subsequent selloff was obvious are hindsight bias.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Be wary of narrative revisionism around event-driven selloffs.

themes.theme: Pain trade and the dot-com analog

insights.claim: Patrick's pain-trade scenario: the NASDAQ bounces toward roughly 29,500 (its Fibonacci retracement zone about 1,000 points higher) but stays below its 50-day, while the S&P 500 reclaims its 50-day and retests its highs, convincing dip-buyers it's all clear before a second leg down.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Don't read an S&P retest of highs as all-clear while NASDAQ stays below its 50-day.

insights.claim: Kevin argues the scariest declines come on the second leg: after the first drop everyone monetizes hedges and gets flat, volatility becomes too expensive to rebuy, and a renewed decline then gets ugly.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Keep some protection through bounces; hedges monetized after leg one leave the market exposed.
insights.quote: the scariest um declines are actually the second time

insights.claim: In the dot-com bust the NASDAQ 100 fell roughly 80-90% from March 2000 to 2002 but had multiple 30-40% rallies and even single 10% up days, so shorting a bursting bubble is not easy.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Expect violent bear-market rallies in AI; size shorts accordingly.
insights.quote: count how many rallies of 30 40% in there

insights.claim: In 2000 the S&P 500 spent about three months retesting its prior high after the NASDAQ topped and did not break below its 50-week moving average until about six months after the dot-com bubble burst, implying the broad market can lag an AI-led top by months.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Broad-market downside may be a January-February event rather than immediate.

insights.claim: Patrick sees very little upside in markets and views rallies as a trap, though the downside may not be immediate and selective names can still work.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Lean defensive/fade rallies but avoid aggressive immediate shorts.
insights.quote: I see very little upside in the markets

insights.claim: Kevin notes that everyone he knows is aggressively buying the dip, which supports the view that the true pain trade is AI weakness spreading to the whole market.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Crowded dip-buying positioning raises downside risk if AI keeps falling.
insights.quote: Everyone I know is buying the dip like with both fists

themes.theme: Fed, CPI and the rates repricing

insights.claim: Credit markets have effectively cut off funding for the AI capex growth engine that drove robust US growth, so expectations of upper-end growth going forward are unrealistic.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Growth estimates tied to AI capex look too high; watch credit spreads for AI borrowers.
insights.quote: the credit markets have basically cut off the AI growth engine

insights.claim: After a hot CPI, fed funds pricing showed about 87% odds of a 25bp hike in December, roughly a one-in-six chance of 50bp, and essentially zero chance of no move.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: December hike is fully priced; 50bp is the tail to watch.

insights.claim: Kevin believes the Fed paused in October to avoid acting before the midterms, likening it to a referee who won't make a marginal call in game seven, and now fears it fell behind given hot CPI, hence 50bp on the table.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Post-midterm Fed is freer to be hawkish; expect catch-up tightening.
insights.quote: They paused because they didn't want to do it in front of the midterms

insights.claim: December 2027 SOFR futures dropped about 38 basis points in three sessions after the inflation print, pricing roughly one and a half additional hikes next year, while December 2027 €STR futures moved only about 15 points.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: US-Europe rate differential widened sharply, a direct driver of dollar strength.

insights.claim: Patrick argues CPI was not a blowout: core was 0.3 for three straight months and headline about 0.4, consistent with recent months and with oil having been near $105, so the market's panic was an overreaction.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Hawkish repricing may be overdone if data merely stays in line.
insights.quote: These weren't blowout numbers

insights.claim: Kevin counters that the last three months of inflation run above the 2024-2025 averages and came when everyone expected re-deceleration, with employment also strong, so the Fed is right to worry.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Sticky inflation plus firm jobs keeps the hiking bias alive.

insights.claim: Kevin expects the classic pattern: the Fed keeps raising rates until something breaks and causes a recession.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Position for eventual policy-induced break; watch financial plumbing for stress.
insights.quote: the Fed raises rates till they break something and then they cause a recession

insights.claim: The US dollar staged a decisive breakout against nearly every currency: euro to fresh lows near 1.10 with 1.08 possible, sterling back to lows, Canadian dollar back to lows, Aussie at roughly six-month lows, and the yen breaking out of a six-week range.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Broad USD strength; short-FX vs USD trend in force, target EUR 1.08.
insights.quote: This is a decisive bull breakout against almost every crossurrency

insights.claim: Whether driven by funding stress or rate differentials, a tightening dollar alongside rising real and nominal rates is a headwind rather than a tailwind for risk assets.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Strong-dollar regime argues for caution on risk assets and commodities.

insights.claim: Patrick calls gold a bear market: lower highs and lower lows after about 60 days of selling, a rejection at the 50-day moving average with no follow-through beyond five days, and fresh lows.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: No basing evidence yet; avoid catching the falling knife.
insights.quote: this is still a bare market. End of story

insights.claim: Patrick's gold downside levels: the 50% retracement of the bull market is 3,600 and the 61.8% is 3,200, near the 2025 consolidation; he would aggressively buy gold in a liquidity washout down there.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Set bids for gold at 3,600 and especially 3,200.
insights.quote: the 50% retracement of this bull market is 3,600

insights.claim: The catalyst that would make Patrick immediately bullish on gold is a Fed pivot away from hawkishness forced by a break in the financial plumbing requiring liquidity provision.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Watch for funding stress and Fed liquidity response as the gold buy signal.

insights.claim: Kevin, a gold bull, cut his position from extra long back to regular long after a failed-breakdown long stopped working as gold sold off while equities rallied, and is more worried about the short term than other gold bulls.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Even committed gold bulls are de-risking; short-term momentum is negative.

insights.claim: Kevin argues Fed tightness is squeezing everything except AI, pushing toward a global recession and forcing selling of small caps and gold, which could help AI bottom and may partly explain falling oil.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Tight Fed may rotate flows back into AI and pressure gold, small caps, oil.
insights.quote: it is squeezing everything except AI

insights.claim: Front-month January crude has only retraced 50% of its bull impulse from June, holding prior highs as support, which Patrick calls a textbook bull-market pullback.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Pullback looks like a buy within an uptrend.
insights.quote: this correction in oil has actually just been a textbook pullback

insights.claim: Global inventories and strategic reserves have been depleted by roughly a billion barrels during the Iran war, so there is no cushion to absorb another supply shock if Iran re-escalates attacks on shipping through the strait.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Any disruption implies outsized upside; hold right-tail oil exposure.

insights.claim: Trump signaled no imminent de-escalation with Iran, and with the midterms past there is little political incentive to suppress oil prices, so moves to $110-$150 are not absurd; $150 in 2008 is about $250 inflation-adjusted.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Upside tail in oil is underpriced by those who find $120-150 absurd.
insights.quote: If oil goes ripping to 110, there's no one that's got a huge political agenda to keep prices down

insights.claim: Kevin is running an oil risk reversal: selling far out-of-the-money puts expiring within days to a week and buying equal dollar value of calls, betting that after a $20 drop the next $10 move is more likely up.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Use downside skew to fund cheap right-tail oil calls.
insights.quote: I'm selling the left tail, buying the right tail

insights.claim: Energy stocks (XLE) pulled back to a Fibonacci retracement and are already turning up, which Patrick sees as a big buying opportunity.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Buy energy equities on this dip.
insights.quote: all this weakness and energy, it's an opportunity
